title: Pando, the one-tree forest
hook: A forest in Utah that is really one tree, joined underground.
peek: In Utah's Fishlake National Forest stands a grove of tens of thousands of aspen trunks. Genetically they are all the same individual, sharing one root system. It is one of the heaviest living things known.
lede: In Fishlake National Forest in Utah, a grove of quaking aspens covers about 43 hectares. It looks like a forest of roughly 47,000 trees. Genetic tests show it is one individual, a male clone whose trunks all rise from a single shared root system. Its name, Pando, is Latin for "I spread", and by weight it is among the largest organisms on Earth.

bullets.text: Aspens often reproduce by sending up new shoots from their roots instead of from seed. Each of Pando's trunks may live a century or so, but the root system keeps sprouting replacements.
Nobody knows exactly how old Pando is. Estimates range from several thousand years to tens of thousands, because the roots have outlived every trunk that could be dated.

bullets.opening: A hillside that turns at once
bullets.text: Because every trunk shares the same genes, the whole clone tends to leaf out together in spring and turn gold together in autumn, so the grove changes colour as a single block.
Deer and elk browse the young shoots, so in parts of the grove few new trunks reach adulthood. Researchers have fenced sections off, and the protected patches are regrowing.
